rangers have pulled more than two hundred saltwater crocodiles

Every year, more swim in.
Doug is going there.

The Dive.
Doug's first stop is a quiet river in northern Australia,
where the water is flat and brown, with no ripples,
no eyes and no movement anywhere.
According to the Queensland Museum, a crocodile resting underwater
can stay down for at least eight hours,
which is a full night's sleep spent lying on the bottom of a river.
One large saltwater crocodile was recorded on a single dive
that lasted eleven and a half hours.
It manages this by barely using any oxygen,
and during a long dive its heart can slow to just two or three beats a minute.
Here's the problem.
Doug watched this river for an hour before deciding that it was empty,
but for a crocodile, an hour is a short dive.
Scientists tested young saltwater crocodiles in water at twenty-eight degrees Celsius,
today's summer temperature, and at up to thirty-five degrees.
Cooler water meant longer dives,
and their time underwater roughly halved for every three and a half degrees of warming.
The crocodile never has to come up to check on Doug,
because it can simply wait.
Doug did not agree to this,
and we've handed him a fishing rod anyway.
Doug announces that the river is empty,
wades in up to his knees, and casts.
Doug has died.
The river was never empty.
It was holding its breath the whole time,
and it can hold it for much longer than Doug can watch.
Noticed.
The Skin.
Look closely at a crocodile's jaw
and you'll see that it's covered in tiny dark dots,
which look like freckles but are something much more useful.
Each dot is a small dome packed with touch sensors.
A two thousand twelve study counted around four thousand of them on an alligator,
mostly on its jaws and inside its mouth.
Nile crocodiles had about nine thousand,
because in true crocodiles the domes cover almost every scale on the body.
The most sensitive domes could pick up forces about ten times smaller
than the most sensitive parts of a human fingertip.
Your fingertip is the most sensitive tool you own,
and a crocodile's face beats it.
Here's the unsettling part.
In an earlier experiment, alligators sat in a tank in complete darkness,
and when a single drop of water hit the surface,
they turned to face the ripples.
In the newer study, once something touched the skin around their jaws,
the animals snapped at it within fifty to seventy milliseconds,
which is about a twentieth of a second.
It doesn't need to see Doug.
It can feel him.
Doug has decided the danger is at the water's edge,
so he's sitting perfectly still in a canoe, in the dark,
in the middle of the river.
One drop falls from his paddle.
Doug has died. Again.
He didn't make a sound,
and one drop was enough.
The Tongue.
A crocodile that spends time in the sea has a problem,
because living in salt water means taking in salt,
and the extra has to go somewhere.
In nineteen eighty-one, two Australian scientists found the answer
on the saltwater crocodile's tongue.
It's covered in salt glands that push the extra salt back out of its body,
and alligators don't have them.
That's part of the reason the saltwater crocodile is one of the most widely spread crocodiles on Earth.
It's found from southern India and Sri Lanka, across Southeast Asia and the Philippines,
east to Micronesia and south to northern Australia.
The Queensland Museum calls it the only crocodile that can survive long journeys at sea.
A United Nations fisheries guide notes that single saltwater crocodiles have turned up
around islands more than a thousand kilometers from the nearest population.
That's nearly half the length of the Great Barrier Reef,
crossed by one reptile, alone, in the open sea.
But here's the twist.
Crocodile experts say it also thrives in fresh water,
in rivers, lakes and swamps as far as hundreds of kilometers inland.
So "saltwater" isn't a nickname,
it's an incomplete list.
Doug has run from the river to the beach
and paddled out on an inflatable ring,
because the sea is where he feels safe.
A crocodile swims calmly past him on its way out to sea,
and it doesn't even look at him.
Doug is fine.
He ran from its river straight into its ocean,
and the only reason he's alive is that it had somewhere else to be.
The Egg.
On a riverbank in the wet season,
there's a large pile of mud and dead leaves that looks like garden waste,
but it's a nest.
The female saltwater crocodile builds the mound herself out of plants,
and in Australia she lays around fifty eggs inside it,
more than four cartons' worth.
Each one weighs about a hundred and thirteen grams,
roughly as much as two large chicken eggs.
The temperature inside the mound decides whether each baby is male or female.
Then the mother stays close,
and the same United Nations fisheries guide says she aggressively protects the nest.
She has reason to worry.
Because nesting happens in the wet season, floods destroy a lot of nests.
Even for the babies that hatch,
the Territory Wildlife Park in northern Australia says only about one percent survive to adulthood.
The strange part comes at the end,
about three months after the eggs are laid,
when the babies start calling from inside their eggs.
When the mother hears them, she digs them out,
and she may gently carry them down to the water in her mouth.
The same jaws that hunt in this river
carry her babies so carefully that they reach the water unhurt.
Doug hears chirping coming from the mound
and leans in close to say hello.
Doug has died.
She can be gentle with that mouth.
She just saves it for family,
and Doug was kneeling on the nursery.
Followed.
The Size.
Saltwater crocodiles are the largest reptiles alive today,
and the true giants are the males.
In Australia, adult females rarely grow longer than three meters,
while males have been reported at twice that length.
In two thousand eleven, a male called Lolong was captured in the southern Philippines.
He measured six point one seven meters,
Guinness World Records named him the largest crocodile in captivity,
and he died in two thousand thirteen.
His title passed to Cassius, a crocodile in Queensland who measured about five and a half meters.
Cassius lived in a crocodile park on an island near Cairns
from nineteen eighty-seven until he died in November two thousand twenty-four.
He had been brought there from the Northern Territory,
and the park believed he had lived well beyond the years of a wild crocodile.
Here's what nobody could measure.
Cassius was thought to be more than one hundred and ten years old.
Nobody knew for sure,
but if that estimate was right,
he hatched around the start of the First World War.
The crocodile Doug is measuring may have been alive longer
than anyone Doug has ever met.
Doug has brought a tape measure to find out how big this one is,
and the tape runs out somewhere around the back legs.
Doug pats it gently on the nose and says hello,
and the crocodile stays asleep.
Doug survives this one.
We had the splash ready.
The tape ran out at the back legs,
and the crocodile did not.
The Home.
When a crocodile becomes a problem, one obvious answer is to take it somewhere far away,
and a study published in two thousand seven tested how well that works.
Australian scientists caught three large males,
fitted each one with a satellite tag,
and moved them away from home.
The biggest, a four and a half meter male,
was flown by helicopter across Cape York, from the west coast to the east,
and released into the sea.
He didn't take the short way back over land.
He swam north, rounded the tip of Cape York,
and came back down the other side,
covering four hundred and eleven kilometers of coastline in twenty days.
That's about twenty kilometers a day, close to a half marathon,
every day for almost three weeks.
He arrived home on Christmas Eve,
and at the time, it was the longest journey home ever reported for a crocodile.
And he wasn't in a hurry to start.
For more than three months, he stayed near the place where he'd been released,
as if he'd settled in, and then he left.
The worst part is that he wasn't special.
All three crocodiles found their way back to where they had been caught.
The scientists concluded that moving a problem crocodile to a remote place
is very likely to be ineffective,
and they called the animals' navigation skills remarkable.
Doug has driven a crocodile a very long way from home,
waved goodbye,
and waited three whole months to be sure it had settled in.
He goes to run a bath.
Doug has died.
The study tracked crocodiles going home.
It did not say whose home,
and this one has apparently picked Doug's.
The Lunge.
On land, size has a cost.
A two thousand nineteen study filmed fifteen species of crocodiles and their relatives
moving at different speeds,
and found that bigger animals moved less athletically on land than smaller ones.

elements.text: LESS ATHLETIC THAN A SMALL ONE

shots.narration: Some crocodiles can gallop,
but for this species, the only report of bounding that the scientists cite
was in young ones under two meters long.
Doug has decided a big crocodile must be a slow one,
so he's climbed onto a branch about as high as a kitchen counter
to eat his lunch in peace.
But that's not where the danger is.
The Northern Territory Government describes the saltwater crocodile's tail as solid muscle
and a major source of power.
It makes the crocodile a strong swimmer,
and it lets it make sudden lunges out of the water to grab its prey.
The same page adds that those muscles let crocodiles move faster than humans on land,
for short bursts.
Less athletic than a small crocodile does not mean slower than Doug.
And Doug has chosen to sit directly above the water,
which is where that tail does its best work.
Doug climbed out of reach.
"Out of reach" was a guess.
Doug takes the first bite of his sandwich.
Doug has died.
Doug's whole plan was about the crocodile on land,
and the crocodile was never on land.
The Roll.
Crocodiles can't chew.
Their teeth are made for gripping, not cutting,
so a meal that's too big to swallow whole is a real problem.
The solution is the death roll.
In a two thousand seven study, scientists filmed young alligators doing it in slow motion.
Each one folded its legs flat against its body,
then bent its head and tail into a curve, like a banana.
Then the whole animal spun along its length,
and when the researchers held the tail still, the alligators couldn't roll at all,
so the tail is doing most of the work.
Large Nile crocodiles have been measured spinning at somewhere between half a turn and one full turn every second.
A two thousand nineteen survey tested crocodiles from every living species,
including thin-snouted species that had been thought unable to do it,
and all but one species rolled.
Here's the part people get wrong.
The crocodile isn't spinning its prey.
It's spinning itself, with its jaws locked shut,
and whatever is in them has no choice but to come along.
Doug has heard of the death roll and assumes it's a dance,
so he's leaning out over the water to get a better look.
He leans a little too far.
Doug has died.
The survey also found that crocodiles roll to escape, not just to feed.
It isn't a dance,
although it does need a partner.
Chosen.
The Legend.
For decades, a famous record book listed one night in nineteen forty-five
as the worst crocodile attack in history.
During the Second World War, around a thousand Japanese soldiers retreated
into the mangrove swamps of Ramree Island, off the coast of what is now Myanmar,
and very few came out.
A naturalist's book from nineteen sixty-two described crocodiles in that swamp at night.
Later writers claimed the crocodiles killed most of the soldiers,
and Guinness repeated the story for years.
The evidence doesn't support it.
In two thousand one, a team of crocodile scientists went back over the records,
and they found that the book's author was apparently not on the island at the time.
Most military histories of the campaign never mention crocodiles.
The team also interviewed older residents who lived there during the war.
They described soldiers dying from combat, disease, hunger and a lack of fresh water,
and the only crocodile deaths they knew of were ten to fifteen soldiers crossing a tidal creek.
Years later, a British historian looked at military records for a documentary
and found that most soldiers had died in combat or drowned.
In late two thousand sixteen, Guinness took the record out of circulation.
Here's the uncomfortable part.
The most famous crocodile attack in history probably didn't happen the way the record book said.
The real danger is quieter: a few people at a time, every year, in many countries.
Doug reads the record book on a rock,
closes it, and feels much better.
Doug is fine.
The legend is not.
The record book got the biggest number wrong,
but the small numbers are still being counted.
The Menu.
Plenty of large animals can kill a person,
but this one belongs on a much shorter list.
Crocodile scientists say that of all the world's crocodiles,
only two species regularly prey on people:
the Nile crocodile and the saltwater crocodile.
The international group of crocodile experts puts it plainly,
saying that saltwater crocodiles prey on people when they get the chance.
The Nile crocodile actually causes more deaths,
so this isn't the deadliest crocodile.
It's just the other one on the list.
A two thousand twenty-one study looked at one province of Indonesia,
East Nusa Tenggara, over ten years.
It counted one hundred saltwater crocodile attacks,
and sixty of them were fatal, which is worse odds than a coin flip.
Most of the people attacked were men, and most of them were fishing.
Even in Queensland, crocodile experts counted thirty-five attacks between nineteen seventy-one and two thousand fifteen.
Here's the disturbing part.
To a large saltwater crocodile, a person isn't a threat to chase off,
and it isn't a case of mistaken identity.
It sees a regular meal.
Doug has written "friend" in his field guide in big letters.
He's offering a handshake from the end of a jetty,
about as close to the water as you can get without swimming.
Doug has died.
He offered his hand to an animal that had already decided what he was,
and it wasn't a friend.
The Comeback.
After the Second World War, crocodile skins were worth a lot of money,
and in northern Australia, hunters shot saltwater crocodiles for their skins,
almost without control, for twenty-six years.
By the time hunting was banned in the Northern Territory, in nineteen seventy-one,
the population there had dropped to about three thousand animals.
Then the crocodiles were protected,
and scientists counted them along the same rivers, year after year, for decades,
and the numbers climbed while the crocodiles got bigger.
Today, crocodile experts estimate there are between eighty and one hundred thousand saltwater crocodiles in the Northern Territory,
close to where the population was before the hunting started.
It's as if a town of three thousand people grew into a city of a hundred thousand within one lifetime.
Worldwide, the species is listed as Least Concern.
Protection worked.
That's the honest part of this story, and it's a real conservation success.
Here's the thing nobody planned for.
The crocodiles have moved back into their old waters,
and that includes the harbor of Darwin, the capital of the Northern Territory.
In two thousand twelve alone, rangers took two hundred and fifteen saltwater crocodiles out of Darwin Harbour.
The Territory's current management plan allows up to one thousand two hundred crocodiles a year to be removed in set areas,
and the traps are still out there.
The most terrifying thing about the saltwater crocodile
is that people nearly wiped it out, then decided to let it live,
and it came back to everywhere it used to be, including the city.
Doug has finally made it to the harbor,
and he's gone for a night swim below the city lights.
He sees all those little lights on the water
and waves at them.
Doug has died.
In the morning, the rangers pull up one of their traps,
and inside is a single red cap.
After all those crocodiles, the rangers caught the cap.
Doug deaths: two hundred and twenty-six.
